questions.q: A company has Authorised Capital of 10,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each. It issued 8,00,000 shares, of which 7,50,000 were subscribed fully paid and 50,000 were subscribed but only ₹8 per share called‑up (₹2 calls in arrears). No forfeited shares. Write the exact line items (with amounts) that will appear under "Share Capital" in the Balance Sheet for this class of shares.
questions.a:
Correct presentation:
Authorised Capital: 10,00,000 shares of ₹10 each = ₹1,00,00,000
Issued Capital: 8,00,000 shares of ₹10 each = ₹80,00,000
Subscribed Capital: 7,50,000 shares of ₹10 each fully paid = ₹75,00,000; 50,000 shares of ₹10 each, ₹8 called‑up = ₹4,00,000 → Total Subscribed = ₹79,00,000
Called‑up Capital: ₹79,00,000
Less: Calls in Arrears (50,000 × ₹2) = ₹1,00,000
Paid‑up Capital: ₹78,00,000
If a student writes "Subscribed Capital ₹80,00,000" they confuse Issued with Subscribed. If they omit the break‑up of fully/partly paid under Subscribed, they miss Schedule III's mandatory disaggregation. If they forget to deduct Calls in Arrears from Called‑up to arrive at Paid‑up, they overstate paid‑up capital.

questions.q: Why does Schedule III require separate disclosure of "Subscribed and fully paid‑up" and "Subscribed but not fully paid‑up" under Subscribed Capital? What would be the impact on a user of financial statements if only a lump‑sum Subscribed Capital figure were shown?
questions.a: Schedule III demands this split because "Subscribed Capital" includes shares shareholders have agreed to take, but "fully paid‑up" means cash has been received for the full nominal value, whereas "not fully paid‑up" means calls are still due (or in arrears). A lump‑sum figure would hide the fact that part of the subscribed capital is not yet paid, misleading investors about the company's actual liquidity and the certainty of future cash inflows. For example, if a company shows Subscribed Capital ₹1 Cr but ₹30 Lakh is in arrears, the true paid‑up capital is only ₹70 Lakh. Without the split, a creditor might overestimate the company's net worth. A student who says "it's just for detail" misses the decision‑usefulness concept (NCERT Class 11: Qualitative Characteristics of Accounting Information → Reliability and Relevance).

questions.q:
TechNova Ltd. has the following data for Equity Shares (₹10 face value):
- Authorised: 20,00,000 shares
- Issued: 15,00,000 shares
- Subscribed: 14,00,000 shares (13,50,000 fully paid @ ₹10; 50,000 partly paid @ ₹8 called‑up, ₹2 in arrears)
- Forfeited Shares: 20,000 shares originally issued @ ₹10, ₹6 paid‑up, re‑issued as fully paid @ ₹8.
Prepare the Share Capital note (Note to Accounts) for the Balance Sheet. Show all calculations.
questions.a:
Step 1: Authorised Capital = 20,00,000 × ₹10 = ₹2,00,00,000
Step 2: Issued Capital = 15,00,000 × ₹10 = ₹1,50,00,000
Step 3: Subscribed Capital:
 Fully paid: 13,50,000 × ₹10 = ₹1,35,00,000
 Partly paid: 50,000 × ₹8 = ₹4,00,000
 Total Subscribed = ₹1,39,00,000
Step 4: Called‑up Capital = ₹1,39,00,000 (same as Subscribed because calls made = ₹8 on partly paid)
Step 5: Calls in Arrears = 50,000 × ₹2 = ₹1,00,000
Step 6: Paid‑up Capital before forfeited = ₹1,39,00,000 - ₹1,00,000 = ₹1,38,00,000
Step 7: Add Forfeited Shares Amount = 20,000 × ₹6 = ₹1,20,000 (amount originally paid‑up on forfeited shares)
Step 8: Total Paid‑up Capital = ₹1,38,00,000 + ₹1,20,000 = ₹1,39,20,000
Balance Sheet Presentation:
Share Capital:
Authorised Capital: ₹2,00,00,000
Issued Capital: ₹1,50,00,000
Subscribed Capital: ₹1,39,00,000
Called‑up Capital: ₹1,39,00,000
Less: Calls in Arrears: ₹1,00,000
Add: Forfeited Shares: ₹1,20,000
Paid‑up Capital: ₹1,39,20,000
Common error: adding forfeited shares at re‑issue price (₹8) instead of original paid‑up (₹6), or forgetting to deduct calls in arrears before adding forfeited amount.

questions.q: Compare the disclosure requirements for "Calls in Arrears" and "Calls in Advance" in the Balance Sheet as per Schedule III. Why is Calls in Arrears deducted from Called‑up Capital to arrive at Paid‑up Capital, while Calls in Advance is NOT added to Paid‑up Capital but shown separately under "Other Current Liabilities"?
questions.a: Calls in Arrears represents amount called by the company but not paid by shareholders; it reduces the actual capital received, so it is deducted from Called‑up Capital to arrive at true Paid‑up Capital. Calls in Advance represents money received from shareholders before the call is made; it is a liability (the company owes the shareholder a future call adjustment or refund) and does not increase paid‑up capital because the call hasn't been made yet. Schedule III shows Calls in Advance under "Other Current Liabilities" (not under Share Capital). A student who adds Calls in Advance to Paid‑up Capital confuses receipt of cash with capital recognition; capital is recognised only when the call is formally made (matching principle). This distinction ensures Paid‑up Capital reflects only capital that has been formally called and is due.

questions.q: A company's Balance Sheet shows "Paid‑up Capital: ₹5,00,00,000" under Share Capital. The Notes to Accounts reveal: "During the last 5 years, the company issued 1,00,000 bonus shares of ₹10 each and bought back 50,000 shares of ₹10 each." An analyst argues that the bonus issue increased Paid‑up Capital by ₹10,00,000 and the buyback decreased it by ₹5,00,000, so the net effect is +₹5,00,000. Evaluate this statement. Is the analyst correct? Why does Schedule III require disclosure of bonus/buyback/non‑cash issues of the last 5 years?
questions.a: The analyst is incorrect in attributing the current Paid‑up Capital figure solely to those two events. The ₹5 Cr Paid‑up Capital is the cumulative result of ALL transactions since incorporation (issues, forfeitures, re‑issues, buybacks, bonus, etc.). The bonus issue of ₹10 Lakh and buyback of ₹5 Lakh are only two events in the last 5 years; the net effect on Paid‑up Capital from these specific events is +₹5 Lakh, but the current balance includes earlier history. Schedule III requires the 5‑year disclosure so users can assess capital structure changes, dilution/accretion trends, and whether the company is returning capital (buyback) or capitalising reserves (bonus). It helps in evaluating earnings per share trajectory and management's capital allocation policy. A student who thinks the current Paid‑up Capital equals the net of last 5 years' events ignores the opening balance and earlier transactions.

questions.q: Design a new scenario (different from the worked examples) where a company has both Equity and Preference Share Capital, with some shares issued for consideration other than cash, some forfeited and re‑issued, and some calls in advance. Write the complete Share Capital section of the Balance Sheet (main head + Note to Accounts) with all Schedule III mandatory disclosures. Include at least one shareholder holding >5%.
questions.a:
A good answer will:
1. Define two classes: Equity (₹10 face) and 8% Preference (₹100 face).
2. Show Authorised, Issued, Subscribed (fully/partly paid), Called‑up, Less Calls in Arrears, Add Forfeited, Paid‑up for EACH class separately.
3. Note to Accounts:
   a. Reconciliation of number of shares (opening, issued for cash, issued for non‑cash, forfeited, re‑issued, buyback, closing) for each class.
   b. Shareholders holding >5% (name, no. of shares, %).
   c. Aggregate of bonus shares, non‑cash issues, buybacks in last 5 years for each class.
   d. Calls unpaid by directors/officers.
   e. Calls in Advance shown under Other Current Liabilities (not in Share Capital).
   f. Terms of conversion for convertible preference shares (if any).
Example skeleton:
Equity: Authorised 50L shares ₹10 = ₹5 Cr; Issued 40L; Subscribed 38L (35L fully paid, 3L partly paid ₹8 called); Calls in Arrears ₹6L; Forfeited 1L shares originally ₹6 paid = ₹6L; Paid‑up = ₹3.5Cr + ₹2.4Cr - ₹6L + ₹6L = ₹3.54Cr? Wait, recalc: 35L×10=3.5Cr; 3L×8=24L; Called‑up=3.74Cr; Less arrears 3L×2=6L → 3.68Cr; Add forfeited 1L×6=6L → 3.74Cr.
Preference: Authorised 10L shares ₹100 = ₹10 Cr; Issued 8L; Subscribed 7.5L fully paid; Forfeited 0.5L originally ₹80 paid = ₹40L; Paid‑up = 7.5Cr + 0.4Cr = 7.9Cr.
Non‑cash issue: 2L equity shares to vendor for machinery.
>5% holder: Promoter Group 10L equity (26.3%).
Calls in Advance: ₹2L (equity) shown under Other Current Liabilities.
This tests ability to synthesise all disclosure requirements simultaneously.
